topics.title: Introduction and standard sets
notes: A set is a collection of distinct elements (no repetition). We say an element belongs to a set using the symbol ∈.
N = natural numbers {1, 2, 3, ...}; Z = integers; Q = rational numbers (p/q, q ≠ 0); I = irrational numbers; R = real numbers.
R = Q ∪ I. Irrational examples: √2, π. Rational examples: -3, 0, 1/3, -5/2.

topics.title: Methods to describe a set
notes: Listing (roster) method: list all members in curly brackets, e.g. A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}.
Property (set-builder) method: describe the members by a property, e.g. A = {x | x ∈ N, x < 5}.
Both methods can describe the same set. Choose the one that is easier to read.

topics.title: Types of sets
notes: Null (empty) set: no elements, written as { } or φ. {φ} is NOT a null set (it has one element, φ).
Singleton set: exactly one element, e.g. {2}. Finite set: elements can be counted (or empty). Infinite set: elements cannot be counted, e.g. N.
Cardinality n(A) = number of elements of a finite set. Example: A = {a, e, i, o, u} gives n(A) = 5.
Subset A ⊆ B: every element of A is in B. Null set is a subset of every set. Every set is a subset of itself. A non-empty set has at least two subsets (φ and itself).
Equal sets A = B: same elements. Equivalent sets: n(A) = n(B). Equal sets are always equivalent, but equivalent sets need not be equal.
Universal set U: superset of all sets under consideration. Disjoint sets: A ∩ B = φ (no common element).

topics.title: Venn diagrams
notes: A Venn diagram shows sets pictorially: the universal set U is the rectangle and every other set is a circle inside it.
Intersecting sets: circles overlap. Disjoint sets: circles do not overlap. Subset A ⊆ B: circle A lies inside circle B. Equal sets: the circles coincide.
Shade the required region to show the answer: union, intersection, complement, difference or symmetric difference.

topics.title: Operations on sets
notes: Union A ∪ B: all elements of A or B (or both). Intersection A ∩ B: only the common elements.
Complement A' = U - A: all elements of the universal set that are not in A.
Difference A - B: elements of A that are not in B. B - A is the reverse. A - B ≠ B - A in general.
Symmetric difference A Δ B = (A ∪ B) - (A ∩ B) = (A - B) ∪ (B - A): elements in exactly one of the two sets.
If A and B are disjoint, then A - B = A and B - A = B.

topics.title: Algebra of sets and laws
notes: Complement laws: A ∪ A' = U, A ∩ A' = φ, (A')' = A, U' = φ, φ' = U.
Identity laws: A ∪ φ = A, A ∩ U = A, A ∪ U = U, A ∩ φ = φ.
Commutative: A ∪ B = B ∪ A and A ∩ B = B ∩ A. Associative: A ∪ (B ∪ C) = (A ∪ B) ∪ C, same for ∩.
Distributive: A ∪ (B ∩ C) = (A ∪ B) ∩ (A ∪ C) and A ∩ (B ∪ C) = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C).
De Morgan's laws: (A ∪ B)' = A' ∩ B' and (A ∩ B)' = A' ∪ B'.
If A ⊆ B then A ∪ B = B and A ∩ B = A.

topics.title: Power set and Cartesian product
notes: Power set P(A): set of all subsets of A (including φ and A). If n(A) = n, then n(P(A)) = 2^n.
Cartesian product A × B: set of ordered pairs (x, y) with x ∈ A and y ∈ B. n(A × B) = n(A) × n(B).
A × B ≠ B × A in general (order matters), but n(A × B) = n(B × A). (A × B) ∩ (B × A) can be non-empty, e.g. when the pairs are (1,1).

short.q: Define a set and give an example of a finite set.
short.answer: A set is a collection of distinct elements. Example: A = {a, e, i, o, u}.

short.q: State the difference between equal sets and equivalent sets.
short.answer: Equal sets have exactly the same elements (A = B). Equivalent sets have the same number of elements, n(A) = n(B).

short.q: Define the symmetric difference of two sets and write its formula.
short.answer: Symmetric difference contains elements in exactly one of A or B. A Δ B = (A ∪ B) - (A ∩ B) = (A - B) ∪ (B - A).

short.q: State De Morgan's laws for two sets A and B.
If n(A) = 3 and n(B) = 2, find n(P(A)) and n(A × B).
If A ⊆ B, find A ∪ B and A ∩ B.
short.answer: A ∪ B = B and A ∩ B = A.

short.q: If A and B are disjoint sets, what is A - B? Give a reason.
short.answer: A - B = A, because A and B have no common element, so nothing of A is removed.
